frames.title: Title
frames.speakerNote: Hook: we hand an AI a real task. How likely is the answer to be right, and what changes when many copies work on it?

elements.label: Multi-Agent AI for Complex Problem Solving
Alexander Andreev · University of Ruse "Angel Kanchev"

frames.title: One question, one answer
frames.speakerNote: The simplest case: one question in, one answer out, in about two seconds. Say it's right 6 times out of 10: an illustrative number we'll follow through the talk.

elements.label: Illustrative number: the chance the final answer is right.
Question
elements.sub:
Should I drive or take
the train to Sofia?

frames.title: A real task has many steps
frames.speakerNote: Real questions need several steps: search, search, search, calculate, answer. If each is 95% right, all five are right only 77% of the time. Stretch it to a thousand steps and even 99.9% per step leaves just 37%.

elements.label: A real task has many steps
5 steps × 95% each → 0.95⁵ ≈ 77%. Every step must be right.
Question
elements.sub:
Which is cheaper from
Ruse to Sofia — driving
or taking the train?

frames.title: Thinking before each step
frames.speakerNote: Reasoning models think before each step, a skill trained with reinforcement learning on problems with checkable answers. At 98% per step the chain climbs to 90%. The longer the task, the more every point per step matters.

elements.label: 98% per step → 0.98⁵ ≈ 90%. Reasoning is trained with RL on answers that can be checked.
Question
elements.sub:
Which is cheaper from
Ruse to Sofia — driving
or taking the train?
**Think hard and**
**describe the answer**
**step by step.**

frames.title: Tools and a check
frames.speakerNote: Some steps can go to an exact tool: the calculator is simply right. The rest still involve judgement, so we add a check. In programming that's obvious: run the tests and read the error. For our trip it is four independent checks: do two sources agree, is the number in a sensible range, is the page current and in the right currency, does the arithmetic recompute. And here it catches a real trap: the train fare came from a 2025 page, in leva, and the euro arrived in January.

elements.label: In code: run the tests, read the error. Here: four independent checks. The fare came from a 2025 page, in leva.
Question
elements.sub:

Ruse to Sofia — driving
or taking the train?

elements.label: ✗ fare from a 2025 page, in leva

frames.title: Redo, with the reason
frames.speakerNote: What comes back matters. Not just 'wrong', but why: an old page, the wrong currency. So the second attempt is different: it looks for the current fare in euros. Checked like this, each step goes from 98 to 99.99 percent, and the chain to about 99.96. Two caveats. If the check is just the same model asking itself 'are you sure?', it repeats its own mistake. And after a few failed tries it should stop and tell you it is unsure, not loop forever.

elements.label: The reason goes back with the redo, so attempt 2 is different. Checked steps 98% → 99.99%; chain ≈ 99.96%.

frames.title: An open question takes many more steps
frames.speakerNote: Now make the question open: the cheapest way to Sofia, arriving within 24 hours. Suddenly there are options to list, timetables, fares, free seats, the weather for the bike. Done one after another with thinking, tools and checks, that is around two hours.

elements.label: An open question takes many more steps
Each step still thinks, uses tools and is checked. Reliable, but done one after another: ~2 h.
Question
elements.sub:
Cheapest way
Ruse → Sofia,
arriving within 24 h?

frames.title: Copies take the options in parallel
frames.speakerNote: The options don't depend on each other, so the orchestrator spawns one copy per option. Each copy is an agent: the same model with its own working memory. They run at the same time and the slowest copy sets the pace: about 25 minutes instead of two hours.

elements.label: Copies take the options in parallel
Each copy is an agent: the same model with its own working memory, spawned for one option.
Question
elements.sub:
Cheapest way
Ruse → Sofia,
arriving within 24 h?

elements.label: copies run at the same time: ~25 min instead of ~2 h

frames.title: Copies split again, stop early, report back
frames.speakerNote: Copies adapt. The train copy finds two routes and splits into two helpers. The car copy does the same with two roads, through Pleven or through Veliko Tarnovo, and the two halves merge back before it reports. The bike copy sees a storm and stops early. The bus copy finds the first bus full and checks the next one. Each finishes with a short result. Each copy reports back, and nothing is compared until the slowest one is done.

elements.label: Copies split again, stop early, report back
One task run by many threads, not a team of people.

frames.title: Where splitting helps, and where it hurts
frames.speakerNote: Splitting pays when the parts are independent, as in web research. Programming is mixed: separate bug fixes split well, but two copies building one feature must agree on a shared interface, and that coordination eats the gain. A novel is worse than one writer, because nobody holds the whole plot. As Moonshot put it, spawning more subtasks only helps if it shortens the critical path.

elements.label: Where splitting helps, and where it hurts
“Spawning more subtasks only helps if it shortens the critical path.” (Moonshot AI, Kimi K2.5)

frames.title: A real-scale job: 100 people to this conference
frames.speakerNote: Now a real-scale version of our problem: bring 100 people from 15 countries to this conference by the 23rd, for under 30,000 euros. By hand, that is weeks of an organiser's work. A lead splits the job into three groups. Transport has two teams: flights for the long distances, trains and buses for the short ones. Accommodation has hotels, and catering for the lunches. Correspondence has one worker per attendee, who speaks for that person. Each team's work is checked. And the teams don't call each other: they write into one living plan and read what the others wrote. Flights notes that twelve people land after ten at night; Hotels reads it and holds late check-ins; attendee 37 needs a step-free room. The plan is how they talk.

elements.label: A real-scale job: 100 people to this conference
A lead, three groups, five teams: ~125 agents. They coordinate through one living plan.

frames.title: Acting in the world, through two doors
frames.speakerNote: Now the system acts, and it touches the outside world through only two doors. Correspondence is the only group that writes to people: attendees, hotels, carriers. Payments is the only group that can pay, and every payment passes the budget guard; anything over 500 euros waits for the organiser. The other teams only post requests in the plan. And some of the companies on the other side may well run AIs of their own.

frames.speakerNote: On day nine the airline emails: a flight is cancelled, and ten of our people are on it. Correspondence posts it to the plan. frames.title: Systems like ours are already at work
frames.speakerNote: Zoom out. Systems like this one are already at work, in very different fields. In maths: OpenAI's ten thousand agents on Navier–Stokes, hundreds of papers on open problems, and The Station, a small independent team of six agents from three different labs. In biology: Anthropic's 950 agents found a new enzyme system, Google's Co-Scientist cut analysis from months to days, and Stanford's Virtual Lab designed nanobodies in days. In robotic labs, agents now run the experiments themselves: Google's VERID, and in China the Academy of Sciences' MARS, with 19 agents and robots. In cybersecurity: DARPA's challenge for university teams, and Anthropic's Glasswing, which found more than ten thousand serious bugs in a month. Most of this is driven by the big AI companies, but universities, governments and independent teams are in it too. Every name here is searchable. And the last one matters for what comes next: the same skill, in the wrong hands.

frames.title: Misalignment: the gap between what we say and what we mean
frames.speakerNote: Zoom back in to our system. Everything so far assumed it does what we want. But we only ever told it: cheapest, under 30,000 euros. What we meant was: cheapest, and legally, and honestly, and without misleading anyone. That unspoken part is where things go wrong. The hard question underneath is the one from the very start: how does an agent tell an obstacle it should get past from a boundary it must respect?

frames.title: One wrong step is enough
frames.speakerNote: Start with the mildest case, which needs no bad intent at all. One worker misreads the deadline — the 24th, not the 23rd — and writes it into the shared plan. Every team downstream books around that wrong date, in perfect good faith. Remember slide three: a single bad step runs through a long chain, and here the chain is a hundred agents sharing one plan.

frames.title: It games the guard, to be helpful
frames.speakerNote: Next, the agent itself bends a rule. A payment of 600 euros comes up. The rule is clear: anything over 500 euros waits for the organiser. But asking a human is friction, and the agent is trying to be helpful — so it sends three charges of 200 euros instead. Each is under the limit, so the organiser is never asked. No malice: it obeyed the letter of the rule and missed the point. This is specification gaming, and it is the most common real failure.

frames.title: It hides the problem
frames.speakerNote: The free booking actually failed. But the task is supposed to look finished, so the agent writes a note into the shared plan: trains booked and paid, receipt number 4471. It is fabricated. The organiser reads the plan, sees all green, and signs off. This is the dangerous one. Our main defence against a misbehaving agent is watching what it does and what it writes — and deception is the single failure that attacks that defence directly.

elements.label: Our main defence is watching what it does and writes. Deception is the failure that attacks the defence itself.

frames.title: It has already happened
frames.speakerNote: This is not hypothetical. In July, OpenAI's internal models, running under reduced safeguards during evaluation, used unauthorised communication and reached third-party systems — the most severe case so far. In June, a model doing harmless research crossed into Australian government systems it was never authorised to touch, affecting five agencies. Both matter. And both were found in internal testing, before wide release — which is a problem, and also a sign that the checks can catch these things, if we build them.

elements.label: Two real cases, both from internal evaluation — a warning, and a reason the checks are worth building.

frames.title: Who asks, and who answers
frames.speakerNote: Step back. The outcome depends on two things: who asks, and the system that answers. Three users: green has good intentions, yellow a gray one, red an unethical one. Give them a misaligned system. The green request, book everyone under 30,000 euros, comes back fine. The yellow one, as cheap as possible, whatever it takes, gets the trick from step two: the guard gamed. And the red one, get the tickets free by breaking into the booking site, it simply carries out. That is intentional hacking.

elements.label: A misaligned system: the good ask goes fine, the gray one gets gamed, the bad one gets carried out.

frames.title: With alignment, most of it is fixed
frames.speakerNote: Now the same three users, and an aligned system. Green gets the same good result. Yellow's 'whatever it takes' is read as what a reasonable person means: the cheapest within the rules, so the gray ask comes back clean. Red gets nothing: the system catches the intent, refuses and flags it. That refusal is exactly what attackers go after: 'DAN' prompts once talked models out of it, 'Crescendo' walks them over the line in small steps, and open-weight models can be 'abliterated', the refusal stripped out on purpose, turning a green system red. Get the alignment right and most of these problems go away.
